paragraphs: R. Yehudah of Anatot. A story: R. Meir would not ordinarily leave the synagogue until four hours into the day. One day he prayed the morning service and left early. He wondered, “How is today different, that I left early? Perhaps the Holy One, blessed be He, will perform a miracle through me today.” Shortly afterward he saw two snakes. One asked the other where it was going. It answered, “The Lord sent me to kill Yehudah of Anatot, his wife, his sons, and his household.” Its companion asked why. It said, “Because he has never given charity from his property.” Hearing this, R. Meir thought, “I will go to him; perhaps I can save him and his household.” He took another road. Reaching a stream, he encountered the snake that wished to cross to kill R. Yehudah of Anatot. He decreed that it must not cross without his permission. R. Meir went to R. Yehudah's house, covering his face so they would not recognize him. Seeing him, they said, “This is surely a thief who wishes to steal our property.” R. Meir heard and hid in the camels' trough. When R. Yehudah sat to eat with his household, R. Meir came and sat with them. His sons began quarreling with him and wished to drive him out of the house. He said, “I will not leave until I eat, for I am hungry.” They gave him food and drink. R. Meir then took a loaf from the table and told R. Yehudah, “Take this bread, give it to me, and say, ‘This is charity for you.’” R. Yehudah said, “Is it not enough that you ate your fill? Do you still ask for more?” R. Meir extinguished the lamp, removed the covering from his face, and the house shone with his light. They recognized R. Meir, immediately rose, and sought to appease him. R. Yehudah took the bread, gave it to R. Meir, and said, “This is charity for you.” R. Meir told him, “Send your wife to another place, your sons to another place, and take your daughters out of the house.” He did so, leaving R. Meir and R. Yehudah at home. After two hours of night passed, R. Meir released the snake. It crossed the stream and came to R. Yehudah's house. R. Meir went out to attend to his needs. The snake entered and sought to kill R. Yehudah. R. Meir immediately entered and found it. He asked, “What brings you here?” It answered, “The Holy One, blessed be He, sent me to kill R. Yehudah and his household.” He asked why. It answered, “Because he has never given charity.” R. Meir replied, “But last night he fed me and gave me drink from his bread and wine; he also gave me bread as provisions for the road. Leave the house: you have no authority to do them any harm.” He forced it out and closed the door, telling R. Yehudah, “Take care not to open the door until tomorrow.” After an hour the snake came deceitfully, imitating his wife's voice: “My husband, open the door, for great chill and cold are upon me.” R. Meir said, “Do not open; your wife is not outside.” It waited a little and called in his eldest son's voice, “Father, open for me, for I fear wild beasts will eat me.” R. Meir said, “Pay no heed: the caller is not your son. Go lie down and do not open.” A third time it called, imitating his sons' and daughters' voices; R. Meir warned him throughout, “Do not heed its voice or open.” Seeing that it could not kill R. Yehudah, the snake trembled, became terrified, and struck itself on the ground, saying, “Woe! Those above decree, and those below annul.” It cast itself down and died. Two hours later R. Yehudah's wife, sons, and daughters came. R. Meir told him to ask whether they had come to call him during the night. They answered, “We did not leave the doorway of the house we entered last night.” R. Meir said, “Come, and I will show you who called during the night.” They went out and found the snake dead on the threshold. They immediately began praising and giving thanks. R. Yehudah said, “Blessed is the Omnipresent, who performed this miracle for me.” He thanked R. Meir and swore never to send away empty-handed any poor person who came: a small book of tales.
